claims.text: Catalytic performance in ethanol oxidation is governed by dynamic formation and removal of a sub-monolayer oxide/hydroxide surface layer.
Reversible surface oxidation optimizes the balance between metallic active sites and oxygenated surface species.
Surface oxygenated species facilitate water activation.
The partially oxidized surface facilitates ethanol dehydrogenation.
The proposed surface balance enables the 12-electron/12-proton ethanol oxidation pathway with enhanced selectivity and durability.
The as-prepared nanoparticles have clean, predominantly metallic PGM surfaces.
A thermal or electrochemical pretreatment can produce a defined sub-monolayer of surface oxide/hydroxide.
The partially oxidized surface layer modulates the electronic structure of the PGM nanoparticles.
The partially oxidized surface layer changes the adsorption energetics of reactants and intermediates.
An optimal fraction of oxidized surface species assists water activation under reaction conditions.
The oxide/hydroxide layer facilitates removal of carbonaceous intermediates.
Removal of carbonaceous intermediates reduces catalyst poisoning.
Reduced poisoning shifts ethanol oxidation toward the complete 12-electron pathway.
Untreated catalysts either under-activate water or become rapidly poisoned by adsorbates.
Pretreatment will increase ethanol oxidation current density relative to the untreated catalyst.
Pretreatment will improve selectivity toward complete ethanol oxidation.
Acetate is presented as an end product representative of complete ethanol oxidation.
Pretreatment will improve durability and reduce signs of catalyst poisoning during prolonged operation.
The pretreatment effect should diminish or vanish at strongly reducing potentials or in nonaqueous media.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis associates complete ethanol oxidation with a 12-electron pathway, but the predicted outcome lists acetate as an example of a complete-oxidation product. Acetate retains the carbon framework and represents partial oxidation rather than the complete 12-electron conversion to CO2/carbonate.
